title: Heat conduction in a bar
summary: Hold the two ends of a steel bar at different temperatures, read the field, then let one face lose heat to the air and watch what a convection boundary does that a fixed temperature cannot.

steps.title: Start a Model
steps.explain: A heat analysis is built from the same Commands as a stress analysis — the Model does not know which one you will run until you add a Step. `model.new` starts an empty one.

steps.title: Show temperatures in degrees Celsius
steps.explain: `model.setUnits` takes a `temperature` entry as well as lengths and forces. The engine works in kelvin underneath; this only changes what the legend and the probe read out. Note that `degC` is an absolute temperature, not a temperature *difference* — the engine tracks the distinction, so `20 degC` and `20 K` are two different things.

steps.title: Add the bar
steps.explain: A one-metre bar of 100 × 100 mm section. Conduction along it is a one-dimensional problem with a closed-form answer, which is exactly what you want the first time you run a solver you have not used before.

steps.title: Give the material a conductivity
steps.explain: Heat needs `k`, the thermal conductivity in W/(m·K) — Fourier's law is `q = −k ∇T`, so without `k` there is nothing to solve. `cp` (specific heat) and `rho` only matter once time enters, in a transient Step; `E` and `nu` only matter if you later ask for stress. Recording all of them now costs nothing.

steps.title: Assign it
steps.explain: As always, a Material only applies to a Body once `material.assign` links them.

steps.title: Mesh it
steps.explain: Conduction has one unknown per node instead of three, so a heat mesh is cheap. 100 mm elements give ten along the bar — plenty, because the exact answer here is linear and even a single linear element reproduces a linear field exactly.

steps.title: Hold the cold end
steps.explain: This is the whole idea of a boundary condition: the equation of conduction says how heat moves *inside* the bar, and says nothing about what the world outside does to it. A boundary condition is that missing information. `constraint.temperature` is the simplest one — a Dirichlet condition, "this face is held at this temperature, whatever it takes".

steps.title: Hold the hot end
steps.explain: The other end at 100 °C. A steady heat problem with no prescribed temperature anywhere is singular: the field would only be defined up to an added constant, and the solve would refuse. One fixed temperature — or one convection face, which you add in a moment — is what makes it well posed.

steps.title: Add a steady heat Step
steps.explain: `procedure: "heat-steady"` solves `∇·(k ∇T) + q = 0`: the state the bar settles into after a long time, with no memory of how it got there. `output: ["temperature"]` asks for the field to be kept.

steps.title: Solve, and read the field
steps.explain: Show the `temperature` field on the mesh. The contours are straight bands at right angles to the bar: the profile is exactly linear, T(x) = 100·x/L, so the middle is at 50 °C and the quarter point at 25 °C. Probe them and check. Reading a temperature field is reading a scalar — there is no direction and no deformed shape, only a value per node, and the legend's two ends are the whole story.

steps.title: Now let a face lose heat to the air
steps.explain: `load.convection` is Newton cooling: the face loses `h·(T − tInf)` watts per square metre to a fluid at `tInf`. Unlike a fixed temperature it does not dictate the face's temperature — it makes the face's temperature part of the answer. `h` is the one number in a thermal model you rarely know well: 5–25 W/(m²·K) for still air, hundreds for forced air, thousands for boiling. State the value you assumed.

steps.title: Solve again with the air in the picture
steps.explain: A second Step with the same two ends held but now with the top face exposed. Solve it and compare with the first: the field is no longer linear and no longer one-dimensional, because heat now leaves sideways as well as along the bar.

steps.title: Run it
steps.explain: Switch the Results panel between the two Steps. The change is small here because the bar is stubby and steel conducts well — the surface loses little compared with what the ends push through. Make the bar thin, or `h` large, and convection takes over completely; that is the fin problem, and the `heated-fin-convection` example is exactly it.

steps.title: The theory you just used
steps.explain: Two laws and two kinds of boundary. Everything else in steady conduction is bookkeeping.
steps.theory:
Fourier's law: the heat flux is proportional to the temperature gradient, $\mathbf{q} = -k\,\nabla T$.
Steady conduction is what you get when nothing accumulates: $\nabla\cdot(k\,\nabla T) + \dot q = 0$.

Two boundary conditions matter here.
Dirichlet (`constraint.temperature`): $T = T_0$ on the face — the world holds it there.
Convection (`load.convection`): $-k\,\dfrac{\partial T}{\partial n} = h\,(T - T_\infty)$ — the face's temperature is part of the answer.
A face with no Command on it is insulated, $\dfrac{\partial T}{\partial n} = 0$: zero flux is the natural boundary condition, so "do nothing" is a real, physical choice and not an omission.

For the bar with two held ends and no source, the answer is the straight line $T(x) = T_0 + (T_1 - T_0)\dfrac{x}{L}$, which any element family reproduces to machine precision. That is why it is the first heat model to build: if it is not exact, something is wrong with the setup, not with the mesh.
